renewal.note: Amazon cancelled Three Pines in March 2023 after one season. Production partners and the streamer reportedly could not reach an agreement on renewal terms despite mutual interest.

bollymeter.basis: Rotten Tomatoes at 72% from 18 critics and Metacritic at 68 from 6 reviews place it in firmly favorable territory; RogerEbert.com called it a collection of intelligent two-hour mysteries for fans of Agatha Christie or Columbo.

pull_quotes.text: A collection of intelligent two-hour mysteries that fans of Agatha Christie or even Columbo should watch.
Handsomely shot snowscapes, a Christmassy setting and Molina's beautifully measured performance make it a moreish winter treat.

seasons.review_body: Three Pines arrived on Prime Video in December 2022 as a prestige adaptation of Louise Penny's beloved Inspector Gamache novels, with Alfred Molina as a casting choice critics consistently praised as the show's strongest asset. The 72 percent Rotten Tomatoes score from 18 reviewers reflected appreciation for the procedural craftsmanship and Molina's measured performance without enthusiasm for the series as a whole. RogerEbert.com called it intelligent Christie-adjacent mysteries. The Telegraph singled out the Quebec snowscapes and Molina's measured work. A running parallel cold case involving a missing Indigenous woman added social weight that critics noted as thoughtful but unevenly integrated. Cancelled after one season despite solid reviews, leaving Penny's expansive book series largely unadapted.

episode_reviews.review_body:
# Three Pines S1E1: "The Hangman - Part 1" Review

*Spoiler-light verdict above. Full episode analysis below.*

A chant demands justice before the case has even settled into shape. The answer keeps coming back with urgency, then the hour cuts toward a quieter accusation: someone is missing, no one is dealing with it, and “no one ever will,” as **Unknown** puts it. That is the pressure underneath “The Hangman - Part 1.” The premiere opens with public anger, then builds a murder puzzle around institutional neglect, forensic detail, and a place with old violence in its soil. It works best when procedure exposes denial, though its emotional charge still outruns its character work.

## Justice First, Answers Later

The first minutes are smart because they avoid a neat corpse-and-clue rhythm. They begin with a demand. “When do we want it?” Unknown asks, and the repetition of immediate justice gives the hour its pulse before the central death investigation locks in. The episode announces its kind of mystery early. Pain has already been waiting. The detective arrives late to it.

That matters because the missing case appears almost immediately as a moral counterweight. Someone says no one is dealing with it, then sharpens the line into the bleaker claim that no one ever will. The wording is blunt. Good. It plants distrust before the procedural engine starts turning. One death gets attention. Another has been left to rot.

The detective confrontation after driving a family home adds a useful aftershock. The episode does not frame that beat as a grand speech. It arrives as workplace friction, one person pressing another about what happened that day. That choice keeps the opening from becoming pure slogan. The case enters through strained human exchange, alongside evidence and official language.

The weakness is shape. The protest, the missing case, and the detective confrontation all carry weight, but the hour has to sprint from public anger to investigation mechanics. The result is forceful, then crowded. Still, as a first move, it gives “The Hangman - Part 1” a spine: justice is loud outside, while the system keeps evading it.

## A Death Disguised as a Freak Accident

The curling match walkthrough is where the episode finds its cleanest procedural hook. **CC de Poitiers** is described as having collapsed while watching a curling match, and the initial version has the odd shape of a freak accident: a public event, a sudden collapse, electrocution. It is a strong mystery image because it puts murder in plain sight and makes the setting part of the trick. A killer does not need a dark alley if a public seat can become the weapon.

The case begins with the language of accident, then grows more deliberate. By the time forensics explains the washer fluid puddle, the bare hands and boots, and an electrified source, the episode has shifted from “how could this happen?” to “who had the patience to stage it?” That shift is the best craft in the premiere. The clues change the category of the death.

The line that the puddle must have been spilled deliberately is the hinge. Washer fluid is mundane, which makes it useful. The episode takes something ordinary and gives it intent. Bare hands and boots matter because the body becomes a circuit. The electric source matters because a public venue becomes a controlled killing field. The details have a satisfying mechanical cruelty.

The murder method is more memorable than the victim’s dramatic presence in this half. That trade-off mostly works for a mystery opener. CC’s death becomes physically legible before she becomes personally vivid, so the emotional investment depends on the investigation and the community’s hostility toward her more than on CC herself.

## The Old Ground Under the Rink

The most charged expansion comes when the murder location is linked to an old residential school for Indigenous kids. The episode does not leave the electrocution as a clever technical problem. It places the death near a site that carries historical harm, and that changes the air around the case. Suddenly the question is not just who engineered the killing. It is why this place, with this history, becomes part of the investigation’s geography.

Here the premiere gains its harder edge. A procedural can flatten places into maps: body here, witness there, evidence there. “The Hangman - Part 1” pushes against that by making the location matter beyond logistics. The old residential school link tells the viewer that the ground has memory, even if the case file wants clean categories.

The tone helps that turn. Dense dialogue around protest and investigation is broken by long stretches of silence near transitions and analytical pivots. Those pauses do real work. They allow the episode to stop performing urgency for a moment and sit with implication. The silence does not solve the exposition problem, but it gives the story space after heavy information lands.

The risk is clear: history can become atmosphere if the writing does not tie it to consequence. In this episode, the link functions as setup. That is acceptable for a first half, but it limits the grade. The hour understands that the murder site should mean something. It has not yet turned that meaning into dramatic action.

## Motive Comes in Through the Side Door

The open question of why so many community figures were upset with CC gives the investigation useful social texture. A staged electrocution requires planning, access, and nerve. Motive has to be wider than a single angry glance. The episode plants that width by implying CC left damage around her, enough for multiple people to matter to the case.

This is also where the structure strains. The murder mechanics are crisp. The motive field is hazier. That may be by design, since this is Part 1, but the hour leans heavily on the promise of upset community figures without giving the same level of specific interpersonal detail that the forensic sequence gets. A puddle, bare hands, boots, a generator, an electrified source: those are concrete. Anger around CC is less concrete in the supplied beats, which makes the emotional map thinner than the physical map.

Still, the episode has a good instinct. It lets the investigation widen through contradictions rather than random suspects. Accident becomes design. A public event becomes a controlled trap. A death scene becomes a social diagram. The detective thread, especially the earlier confrontation about what happened while driving a family home, keeps authority under pressure too. The people solving the case are part of the moral atmosphere they are trying to read.

The best choice is restraint. The premiere does not make every grievance equally loud. It withholds. That helps the mystery, though it also leaves this half feeling like a technical demonstration waiting for fuller character heat.

## The Brooklyn Photo Opens a Second Wound the episode produces a photo from two weeks earlier in a Brooklyn housing project. The effect is immediate because it yanks the story out of the local murder pattern and back toward the missing case. **Blue Two-Rivers** becomes the emotional reversal point when the evidence suggests survival. Unknown’s shocked “She’s alive?” gives the turn its cleanest human beat.

That late move matters for the episode’s architecture. The hour starts with public demands for justice, detours through a bizarre electrocution, then returns to the abandoned missing person thread with a live possibility. It is the right kind of Part 1 ending because it reorders attention. The murder of CC remains the central puzzle, but Blue’s photo insists the neglected case has not stayed buried.

Then comes the sudden statement that CC de Poitiers is no longer there. As an ending beat, it has a crisp vanishing quality. The episode has spent time converting CC from a public collapse into a deliberate murder victim. Now the idea that she is “no longer there” adds a new instability to the investigation. The body, the place, and the old assumptions all become less secure.

The criticism: the hour’s two engines do not yet run at equal power. The Blue thread has moral force. The CC thread has forensic snap. The best version of the show will make those strengths collide instead of alternating between them. This premiere plants that possibility with confidence. It has not cashed it in yet.

## The Verdict

“The Hangman - Part 1” is a solid, tense opener built around an apparent accident that becomes a deliberate killing, while an ignored missing case refuses to stay ignored. The forensic construction of CC’s electrocution is the hour’s strongest material, especially the way ordinary details become instruments of murder. The protest opening and the residential school link give the case moral pressure beyond puzzle mechanics.

The episode is less convincing when motive and character need to carry the same charge as the evidence. The community anger around CC is planted, but not textured enough to match the precision of the washer fluid and power-source clues. Even so, the final Brooklyn photo gives the hour a strong second pulse. As a season starter, it earns attention by making procedure answer to history, neglect, and consequence.

verdict.one_liner: A tense opener with sharp forensic craft, stronger on method than motive, and lifted by its neglected missing-case thread.
